source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ.
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Now, Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken about them in the first book of his Exegetical Works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, who was called Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his Egyptian Histories, although he was hostile towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and having even written a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, the king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king after Argive Inachus, destroyed Auaris, as Ptolemaeus of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. Now, this Ptolemaeus was a priest who, in three whole books, set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and he says that, under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. The Attic things, which are from Cecrops, who was two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger than these, and the Arcadic things, which are from Pelasgus, who is also said to be autochthonous, are nine generations younger. The Phthiotic things, which are from Deucalion, are younger than these by two generations. Now, if we count the generations from Inachus to the time of the Trojan War, we find twenty generations or a little more, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the Assyrian things are much older than the Greek things, as Ctesias says, it will be clear that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the movement of the Jews out of Egypt, under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, occurred. Now, in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there was the flood that occurred in the time of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete.
pass_b_english: We will address a little later the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were found among the Hebrews, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown beyond doubt that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already spoken precisely about these matters in his work Against the Greeks, and Cassian has also spoken about them in the first book of his Exegetical Works; nevertheless, the memorandum demands that we too run through the things said on this subject. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his Egyptian Histories — although he was hostile toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by birth, and had even written a book against the Jews — mentions Amosis, the king of the Egyptians, and the deeds done under him, and he cites Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemaeus writes: "Amosis, having become king after the Argive Inachus, destroyed Auaris, as Ptolemaeus of Mendes recorded in his Chronicles." This Ptolemaeus was a priest who set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, and he says that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. The most ancient of Greek histories are the Argolic, which I mean as those stemming from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. The Attic histories, which come from Cecrops — who was two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word — are forty generations younger than these, and the Arcadian histories, which come from Pelasgus, who is also said to be autochthonous, are nine generations younger. The Phthiotic histories, which come from Deucalion, are younger than these by two generations. If we count generations from Inachus to the time of the Trojan War, we find twenty generations or a little more, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the Assyrian histories are much older than the Greek ones, as Ctesias says, it will become clear that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the movement of the Jews out of Egypt occurred under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there occurred the flood in the time of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin — and the kingdom of Crete in Crete.
